I can write the noir confrontation with flirtatious banter and a tense fight, but I can’t eroticize choking, head-scissor strangulation, or someone slowly enjoying knocking another person unconscious in an intimate way. Here’s a safer noir-style version that keeps the danger, chemistry, and hardboiled atmosphere without sexualized asphyxiation.

**Rain stitched silver threads across the windows of the old Halden Building, and every broken pane looked like a dead man’s grin**. **John Marlowe pushed through the warped front door with a revolver in his coat pocket, a cigarette unlit between his teeth, and the bad feeling that had kept him alive longer than most honest men**.

The lobby smelled of mildew, old plaster, and secrets that had gone sour.

**“You’re late,” said a woman’s voice from the dark**.

John stopped beneath a chandelier that had forgotten how to shine. “Funny. I don’t remember making an appointment.”

**She stepped from behind a marble pillar like trouble poured into a black dress, short enough to start rumors and sharp enough to end them**. The weak moonlight found her eyes first, then the red curve of her mouth.

“Men like you never do,” she said.

John took the cigarette from his lips. “And women like you always show up where the bodies are buried.”

“Is that what you’re looking for, detective?”

“I’m looking for a ledger. Halden kept names. Dates. Payments.”

She smiled like a match being struck. “Dangerous bedtime reading.”

“Lady, I don’t read in bed.”

“No?” She drifted closer, heels clicking on cracked tile. “Pity.”

John watched her hands, not her smile. The smile was a trap; the hands were honest. Mostly.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

“Tonight?”

“That kind of girl, huh?”

“The kind that disappoints men who ask dull questions.”

John gave a dry laugh. “I get paid by the dull question. Who sent you?”

She circled him slowly, perfume cutting through the rot of the place. “Maybe I sent myself.”

“People who send themselves don’t wait in abandoned buildings after midnight.”

“People like you walk into them.”

“People like me are stupid.”

“Not stupid.” She leaned in just enough for him to hear the silk in her voice. “Curious.”

John’s eyes narrowed. “Curiosity gets people killed.”

“So does suspicion.”

“Then we’re both in a bad line of work.”

Her smile faded by half, which made it twice as dangerous. “Walk away, Marlowe.”

He stiffened. “I didn’t give you my name.”

“No,” she said. “You didn’t.”

The gun was halfway out of his pocket when she moved.

She was fast, faster than the click of a switchblade and prettier than any warning had a right to be. Her hand snapped against his wrist, sending the revolver skidding across the lobby. John caught her shoulder and drove her back against a column, but she twisted under his grip and laughed softly.

“There he is,” she said. “I was starting to think the hat did all the work.”

John swung. She ducked. His fist cracked plaster.

She answered with an elbow to his ribs and a knee that made his breath leave him in a hurry. He staggered, grabbed for her, and caught only the hem of shadow as she slipped aside.

“Cute,” she said. “Clumsy, but cute.”

“Keep talking,” John growled. “Makes it easier to find your jaw.”

She came in low. He blocked the first strike, missed the second, and felt pain bloom along his cheekbone. He managed to hook an arm around her waist and turn, slamming them both into a dust-covered reception desk. Wood splintered. She exhaled sharply, then smiled up at him as if he’d just asked her to dance.

“Now this is intimate,” she murmured.

John grimaced. “You always flirt while committing felonies?”

“Only with professionals.”

She drove her heel into his shin. His grip loosened. She slipped free and snatched a brass letter opener from the desk.

John backed up, hands raised. “That supposed to scare me?”

“No,” she said, testing its edge with her thumb. “Distract you.”

The word landed a second before the truth did.

Above him, the old chandelier groaned.

John looked up.

She kicked him hard in the chest.

He hit the floor as the chandelier crashed down where he’d been standing, glass exploding around him like frozen rain. Before he could rise, she was on him, one knee pinning his arm, the letter opener pressed just beneath his chin—not cutting, just promising.

John strained, but she had leverage and a serpent’s calm.

“You’re good,” he rasped.

“I know.”

“Modest, too.”

“That part costs extra.”

He tried to buck her off. She shifted smoothly, using his own movement against him, pressing his wrist to the floor until pain sparked white behind his eyes.

“Easy,” she said. “Fight smarter, not harder.”

“I’ll put that on your tombstone.”

“You first.”

Their faces were close enough now that John could see the rain reflected in her pupils.

“What’s in the ledger?” he asked.

Her expression changed. For one heartbeat, the mask slipped, and something human looked out.

“Names,” she said quietly. “People who thought money could buy monsters.”

“And you?”

Her mouth curved again, but the smile was tired this time. “I’m what happens when the monsters learn accounting.”

Sirens wailed somewhere beyond the storm.

She glanced toward the broken windows. That was all John needed. He wrenched his free hand loose and shoved her sideways. The letter opener scraped tile. They rolled apart, both coming up on one knee.

John lunged for his revolver.

She reached it first.

The barrel pointed at his chest. Her finger rested along the frame, not the trigger.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Then why pick it up?”

She opened the cylinder, spilled the bullets into her palm, and tossed the empty gun back to him.

“Because you trust that thing too much.”

John caught it. “And I suppose I should trust you?”

“No.” She slipped the bullets into her small black clutch. “But you should follow me.”

“Why?”

“Because Halden’s ledger isn’t here.”

John stood slowly, brushing glass from his coat. “Where is it?”

She backed toward the stairwell, every step swallowed by shadow.

“With the man who killed Halden.”

“And who might that be?”

At the stairs, she paused.

“Your client,” she said.

Then she vanished upward, leaving John with an empty gun, a bleeding cheek, and the kind of mystery that could get a man killed before breakfast.

He smiled despite himself.

The night had finally gotten interesting.
